metadata.research_goal: Create backend-ready volleyball coaching knowledge for setting mechanics, offensive organization, attacking mechanics, attack choices, system logic, progressions, tactical rules, physical demands, and load risks using official FIVB/USA Volleyball sources and peer-reviewed match-analysis and biomechanics research.

source_refs.title: FIVB Coaches Manual Level II
source_refs.notes: Used for offensive system definitions, 5-1 and 6-2 logic, set numbering and height/speed model, combination play principles, physical demands, and common volleyball injury areas.

source_refs.title: FIVB Official Volleyball Rules 2025-2028
source_refs.notes: Used for legal constraints on back-row attack, attack line takeoff, front-zone attacks, and libero overhand setting restrictions.

source_refs.title: Thoughts for Setters
source_refs.notes: Used for setting error margins, hitter-friendly set ranges, safe misses, avoiding tight/low/outside sets, and game-like setter repetition.

source_refs.title: Recipe for a Setter
source_refs.notes: Used for setter attributes, the concept of bettering the ball, front-row setter demands in a 5-1, and 6-2 setter/hitter implications.

source_refs.title: The 7 Speeds of Volleyball
source_refs.notes: Used for reading speed, decision speed, reaction speed, jump setting, neutral presentation, and setter choice under time pressure.

source_refs.title: Teach Your Players to Hit More Effectively
source_refs.notes: Used for attacker range, line/cross-body options, off-speed shots, hitting over and off the block, and training against live blockers.

source_refs.title: Creating Talent with What You Have
source_refs.notes: Used for out-of-system development concepts, including training non-setters to deliver hittable balls from random locations.

source_refs.title: Tactical Determinants of Setting Zone in Elite Men's Volleyball
source_refs.organization_or_author: Afonso, Esteves, Araujo, Thomas, and Mesquita
source_refs.notes: Used for the relationship between serve/reception constraints and setting zone in elite side-out, including the effects of deep jump serves, reception zone, receiver role, and low receptions.

source_refs.title: The Interpersonal Coordination Constraint on the Volleyball Setter's Decision-Making on Setting Direction
source_refs.organization_or_author: Denardi, Clavijo, Santana, Oliveira, and Correa
source_refs.notes: Used for the concept that setter direction is constrained by attacker-block spatial relationships and movement dynamics, not only by a pre-called play.

source_refs.title: Match Analysis in Volleyball: a Systematic Review
source_refs.organization_or_author: Silva, Marcelino, Lacerda, and Vicente Joao
source_refs.notes: Used for framing volleyball performance analysis around skill interactions, match phase, player position, and predictive indicators rather than isolated technique.

source_refs.title: The Setter's Attack in High-Level Volleyball
source_refs.notes: Used for setter attack logic, especially that setter attacks are more favorable after high-quality passes and can increase offensive variability.

source_refs.title: Analysis of the Attack Tempo Determinants in Volleyball's Complex II
source_refs.notes: Used for transition offense logic: dig type, dig efficacy, and setting zone help determine attack tempo after defensive plays.

source_refs.title: Determinant Factors of Attack Efficacy in High-Level Male Volleyball
source_refs.notes: Used for attack efficacy logic, including the value of high-quality reception, first-tempo attack, hard-driven attack, setting type, and attack direction.

source_refs.title: Upper Limb Biomechanics During the Volleyball Serve and Spike
source_refs.notes: Used for spike phase modeling, overhead shoulder load, and the principle that different attack/serve types place different kinetic demands on the shoulder.

source_refs.title: Ball-To-Hand Contact Forces Increase Modeled Shoulder Torques during a Volleyball Spike
source_refs.notes: Used for spike shoulder-load risk, ball-contact force, and the need to monitor swing volume and recovery in adolescent and developing attackers.

source_refs.title: Biomechanical Improvements in Performance and Injury Prevention in Volleyball Spikes: Effects of a 4-Week Training Program
source_refs.notes: Used for spike jump and landing training implications, including lower-limb coordination, ground reaction force, center-of-mass control, and safer landing mechanics.

source_refs.title: Volleyball Attack Names and Set Calls
source_refs.notes: Used only as supporting terminology for common attack names such as quick, gap/31, back-1, slide, bic/pipe, and D; tactical principles were cross-checked against official and peer-reviewed sources.

key_concepts.concept: The setter's job is to improve the team's offensive state on the second contact.
key_concepts.details: A good set is not only technically clean. It converts the first contact into a hittable ball, preserves available attackers, manages blocker information, and gives the attacker an appropriate range, height, and tempo.

key_concepts.concept: Setter footwork should beat the ball to the setting window whenever possible.
key_concepts.details: The setter reads the first contact early, releases to the ball, uses efficient shuffle, crossover, drop, or run-through movement, and attempts to arrive balanced before contact. When arrival is late, the priority shifts from perfect mechanics to a hittable, legal, safe location.

key_concepts.concept: Neutral body and hand presentation preserves options and delays the block.
key_concepts.details: A setter who can front set, back set, jump set, or attack from a similar posture makes blockers wait longer. Deception should never cost location quality at beginner or intermediate levels.

key_concepts.concept: Hand setting uses legs, trunk stability, shoulder positioning, wrists, and fingers as a coordinated chain.
key_concepts.details: The hands receive the ball above the forehead or slightly in front of the face, fingers shape around the ball, elbows remain elastic, and the release is created by coordinated extension rather than a slap or catch.

key_concepts.concept: Set location should be coached as a target range, not a pinpoint dot.
key_concepts.details: The hitter needs a usable window in width, depth, and height. For high sideline balls, safe error is generally high, slightly inside the antenna, and off the net rather than tight, too low, over the net, or outside the antenna.

key_concepts.concept: Tempo is the relationship between setter contact, ball flight, and hitter approach timing.
key_concepts.details: A first-tempo attack depends on the hitter already committing near setter contact. Slower tempos give the hitter more time but give blockers and defenders more information.

key_concepts.concept: Offense changes when the setter can operate from the target zone versus when the team is out of system.
key_concepts.details: In-system offense can use middle quicks, slides, faster pins, pipe, setter attack, and combinations. Out-of-system offense should prioritize high, hittable balls, court spacing, legal setter alternatives, and low-error attacking choices.

key_concepts.concept: Side-out and transition offense start from different constraints.
key_concepts.details: Side-out begins after serve receive and often has more planned organization. Transition begins after a dig or block touch, so attack tempo is constrained by dig quality, setter zone, attacker recovery, and spacing.

key_concepts.concept: The 5-1 and 6-2 systems trade setter consistency, front-row attack numbers, substitution needs, and player specialization.
key_concepts.details: A 5-1 gives one setter full offensive control and consistent hitter-setter relationships. A 6-2 can provide three front-row attackers when the back-row setter runs the offense, but it requires two setters who can coordinate and often front-row setters who can also attack or be substituted.

key_concepts.concept: Attacking is not just arm swing power; it is approach timing, jump location, blocker reading, and shot selection.
key_concepts.details: The attacker must coordinate approach, penultimate step, takeoff, arm preparation, contact point, and post-contact landing while reading set quality, block shape, floor defense, and match context.

key_concepts.concept: The penultimate and final block step convert approach momentum into vertical impulse and body control.
key_concepts.details: A useful approach accelerates into a longer, lower penultimate step, then uses the final plant/block step and arm drive to redirect horizontal speed upward without drifting under the net.

key_concepts.concept: A high, slightly in-front contact point gives the attacker more shot choices.
key_concepts.details: Contact behind the head, across the body, too low, or too tight to the net reduces power and makes the attacker predictable or vulnerable to blocks. Strong attackers can still convert imperfect sets through roll shots, tips, tooling, or recycling.

key_concepts.concept: Attackers need line, cross-court, sharp angle, seam, high hands, wipe, roll, tip, and recycle options.
key_concepts.details: Training only hard cross-court swings creates predictable hitters. Attackers should learn to score or keep pressure with varied shots from both good and poor sets.

key_concepts.concept: Offensive combinations are designed to manipulate blocker timing and spacing.
key_concepts.details: Quicks, slides, crossing patterns, reverse patterns, pipe, and pin tempo can create one-on-one attacks, split seams between blockers, or force end blockers to reach away from the court.

key_concepts.concept: Back-row status, libero actions, and attack-line position directly shape legal attack choices.
key_concepts.details: Back-row attackers must respect attack-line takeoff rules when contacting above the net. A libero's overhand finger set from the front zone restricts a teammate from completing an above-net attack from that ball.

technical_models.name: Setter ready, release, footwork, and contact model
phases: pre-contact scan: identify pass quality, first-contact angle, setter-base location, available attackers, and blockers
release: move as soon as the first-contact path is readable while avoiding overlap or teammate collision
movement: use shuffle for short lateral adjustment, crossover or run-through for longer balls, drop step for balls behind, and emergency platform set when hand set is unrealistic
arrival: stop or slow enough to create a stable base, keep hips and shoulders organized, and keep options available
contact: set above the forehead or slightly in front when possible, with hands prepared early and body balanced
recovery: cover the attack, prepare for blocker touch, or transition to defense
coaching_cues: arrive balanced when the pass allows it
make the next ball better than the last touch

common_errors_and_corrections.error: Setter waits to see the full pass before moving.
common_errors_and_corrections.correction: Train first-contact reading and immediate release on pass trajectory, not on ball arrival.

common_errors_and_corrections.error: Setter overruns the ball and sets while drifting.
common_errors_and_corrections.correction: Use shorter last steps, stop-hop, or jump set only after the setter can control body momentum.

common_errors_and_corrections.error: Setter squares too early to one target and exposes the set.
common_errors_and_corrections.correction: Teach neutral posture first, then add deception only after location accuracy is stable.

common_errors_and_corrections.error: Setter forces hands on a low or wide ball.
common_errors_and_corrections.correction: Allow a legal forearm set or controlled bump set when the ball cannot be handled cleanly overhead.

progression.beginner: Self-toss and partner setting with simple footwork, then target setting from easy passes.
progression.intermediate: Random pass locations, front/back set options, jump-stop arrival, and decision calls after pass quality grades.
progression.advanced: Jump setting, late blocker reads, setter attack threat, transition setting, and deceptive but repeatable release.

technical_models.name: Hand setting mechanics and release model
components: base: feet active, knees flexed, trunk stable, weight able to move through the ball
hands: early window above forehead, fingers spread around the ball, thumbs and index fingers forming a natural setting shape
contact: brief, elastic contact with finger pads and hands cushioning symmetrically where possible
release: coordinated extension through legs, hips, trunk, shoulders, elbows, wrists, and fingers
direction: body and hand angle direct the ball without excessive spin, carry, or double contact risk
finish: hands extend toward the intended target while the setter lands or recovers in control
coaching_cues: set through the ball, not at it

common_errors_and_corrections.error: Flat hands or palms contact the ball.
common_errors_and_corrections.correction: Use wall-setting and close partner setting with a finger-pad contact constraint.

common_errors_and_corrections.error: Ball is contacted too low or beside the head.
common_errors_and_corrections.correction: Move feet first and require contact above the forehead in low-speed reps before adding randomness.

common_errors_and_corrections.error: Release comes only from the wrists.
common_errors_and_corrections.correction: Add leg-drive rhythm and freeze-finish tasks to link lower body and hands.

common_errors_and_corrections.error: Back set telegraphs through early arching or turning.
common_errors_and_corrections.correction: Train front and back release from the same neutral window at short distance before increasing speed.

technical_models.name: Set location and safe miss model

locations.target_principle: High enough for a full approach, inside the antenna, and off the net so the hitter can see and swing.
locations.safe_miss: higher, slightly inside, or deeper off the net
locations.danger_miss: too tight, too low, outside antenna, or over the net

locations.target_principle: Give the hitter space to approach from the right side and contact in front of the hitting shoulder.
locations.danger_miss: short into the antenna lane, tight to the net, or crossing the hitter's body

locations.target_principle: Low, fast, and close to the setter's release window only when pass and hitter timing support it.
locations.safe_miss: slightly higher or withheld to another attacker
locations.danger_miss: forcing quick when the middle is late, broad jumping, or screened by the setter

locations.target_principle: Fast enough to punish a committed middle blocker but high enough for the back-row attacker to take off legally and contact in rhythm.
locations.safe_miss: slower and higher when the hitter is late
locations.danger_miss: too low, too tight, or timed so the hitter jumps from on or over the attack line

locations.role: middle attacker moving behind the setter, usually one-foot takeoff
locations.target_principle: Back-set path leads the middle into a one-foot attack lane without drifting into the antenna or blocker.
locations.danger_miss: too far outside, too tight, or too low for the moving hitter

technical_models.backend_use: Use this model to tag set location goals, setter accuracy metrics, and hitter error context.

tempos.hitter_timing: Hitter is already in the jump or final approach phase at or just before setter contact.
tempos.best_use: Excellent pass, middle available, setter balanced, blockers must be held.
tempos.risk: High timing error if pass drifts or hitter is late.

tempos.hitter_timing: Hitter is usually in the middle or late approach steps as the setter contacts the ball.
tempos.best_use: Good pass, coordinated hitter-setter relationship, need speed without first-tempo risk.
tempos.risk: Can trap the hitter if the ball is low or the hitter's approach angle is poor.

tempos.hitter_timing: Hitter reads setter contact while already building approach speed; relationship varies by program.
tempos.best_use: Intermediate to advanced offense where multiple attackers can arrive in rhythm.
tempos.risk: Requires shared language and many setter-hitter repetitions.

tempos.hitter_timing: Hitter starts or adjusts approach after reading the ball's arc.
tempos.best_use: Out-of-system, beginner offense, poor pass, or when preserving low-error attack is more important than blocker delay.
tempos.risk: Blockers have more time to form a double or triple block.

common_errors_and_corrections.error: Fast tempo is added before location and hitter timing are stable.
common_errors_and_corrections.correction: Require a high percentage of hittable high and medium tempo balls before lowering set height.

common_errors_and_corrections.error: Hitter waits for quick set to appear before starting.
common_errors_and_corrections.correction: Train quick attackers to commit to the approach based on pass and setter position, with the setter choosing whether to deliver.

common_errors_and_corrections.error: All attackers run the same tempo regardless of pass quality.
common_errors_and_corrections.correction: Use pass-quality calls to automatically expand or shrink the offense.

technical_models.name: Out-of-system second-contact protocol
decision_order: If the setter can legally and safely take the second contact in control, let the setter set.
If the setter took the first contact or cannot reach the ball, the nearest trained non-setter owns the second contact early and loudly.
If the ball is below hand-setting height or moving too fast, use a platform set or controlled emergency contact.
Prioritize a high, hittable ball to the best available outlet, commonly left pin, right pin, or a high back-row option.
Keep the ball off the net and inside the court. Do not aim for a perfect antenna set from a poor body position.
Attacker chooses a high-percentage swing, shot, tool, or recycle based on block and set quality.
training_constraints: Every player practices second-contact setting from random digs.
Out-of-system targets should be large zones, not small hoops.
Coach scores the quality of the next attack opportunity, not just whether the set hits the target.

common_errors_and_corrections.error: Non-setters panic and send a tight free ball.
common_errors_and_corrections.correction: Train a default high outlet call with a clear target zone several feet off the net.

common_errors_and_corrections.error: Setter tries to take impossible second contacts and removes court coverage.
common_errors_and_corrections.correction: Install a help call and rehearse setter-first-contact scenarios.

common_errors_and_corrections.error: Out-of-system hitter swings as if the set were perfect.
common_errors_and_corrections.correction: Teach hitters to expand the attack menu: high hands, roll deep, tip short, tool, or recycle.

technical_models.name: Setter decision tree
inputs: setter court position and body control
available attackers and their approach timing
opponent middle blocker location and commitment
back-row attack availability and legal takeoff space
hot hitter or struggling hitter state
decision_steps: Can I legally and cleanly take the second contact? If no, call help early.
Is the pass in the excellent or acceptable setting zone? If yes, keep at least two or three attackers alive.
Is the middle on time and the opponent middle block vulnerable? If yes, quick or quick-decoy options are live.
Is the opponent middle committing or drifting? If yes, use pin, slide, pipe, or opposite choices that punish that movement.
Is a hitter in a favorable one-on-one or late-block situation? If yes, favor that hitter if the set can be delivered accurately.
Is set quality at risk? If yes, choose a safer high ball or outlet rather than forcing tempo.
Is the setter attack available after a high-quality pass and uncommitted block? If yes, use sparingly as a variability tool.
After the play, update tendencies: who scored, who was stopped, where blockers cheated, and which pass qualities allowed each option.
technical_models.backend_use: Can drive tactical prompts, drill randomization, and in-app setter IQ assessments.

technical_models.name: 5-1 offense
technical_models.structure: Five attackers and one setter. The same setter runs the offense in all six rotations.
strengths: front-row setter can attack or dump
constraints: three front-row rotations have only two front-row attackers if the setter is front row
setter must block and defend at the net when front row
front-row setter height and blocking ability matter
back-row attack and combinations become important to maintain pressure
best_for: teams with one clearly superior setter
teams prioritizing consistency and offensive control
intermediate and advanced teams with back-row attack options

technical_models.name: 6-2 offense
technical_models.structure: Two setters are used. The back-row setter runs the offense while the front-row setter is available as a hitter or is substituted.
strengths: creates more pin and middle pressure at the net
uses setters who can also attack
can protect a shorter setter from front-row blocking demands
constraints: requires two setters with compatible location standards
substitution rules and rotation management become more complex
setter-hitter connections may be less consistent
team needs disciplined serve-receive and transition switching
best_for: intermediate to advanced teams that can manage rotation complexity

technical_models.name: Attack approach, penultimate, arm swing, contact, and landing model
phases: read: identify pass, setter body, set trajectory, block shape, and open court
approach start: time the first step to the set tempo and maintain an angle that opens the court
penultimate step: longer and lower step that helps convert horizontal speed into vertical jump
block step and arm drive: final plant and coordinated arm swing help redirect force upward
takeoff: jump with control, avoid drifting into the net or under the ball
arm preparation: create shoulder and trunk loading without excessive shoulder strain or loss of timing
acceleration: sequence trunk rotation, shoulder internal rotation, elbow extension, and hand speed
contact: reach high and slightly in front, contact with a firm hand, and direct the ball based on target choice
follow-through: decelerate the arm and land balanced on two feet when possible
coverage/recovery: prepare for block touch, dig transition, or next movement
coaching_cues: see the set before full commitment unless running first tempo
last two steps create the jump
jump behind the ball, not under it
land in control before celebrating or recovering

common_errors_and_corrections.error: Approach starts too early and hitter reaches behind the body.
common_errors_and_corrections.correction: Use tempo-specific start cues and require the hitter to see the set peak for high balls.

common_errors_and_corrections.error: Approach is straight into the net.
common_errors_and_corrections.correction: Rehearse angle approaches that preserve court vision and reduce centerline/net drift.

common_errors_and_corrections.error: Penultimate step is short and upright.
common_errors_and_corrections.correction: Use approach-jump drills emphasizing a longer, lower next-to-last step and aggressive arm drive.

common_errors_and_corrections.error: Arm swing is all shoulder with little trunk or lower-body contribution.
common_errors_and_corrections.correction: Train approach timing, trunk rotation, medicine-ball sequencing, and controlled overhead volume.

common_errors_and_corrections.error: Hitter lands on one foot or drifts into blockers.
common_errors_and_corrections.correction: Reduce approach speed and rebuild takeoff/landing mechanics before increasing tempo or net height.

technical_models.name: Attack choice decision model
inputs: set quality: perfect, hittable, tight, off-net, too fast, too slow, or out-of-system
block: no block, single, late double, formed double, triple, hands high, hands drifting, seam open
defense: perimeter, rotational, off-block coverage, short defender, deep defender, line defender, cross-court defender

choices.best_when: hitter is balanced, cross seam or court is available, and contact is high enough to clear the block
line block is late, outside hand is reachable, or defender has shifted cross-court
set is inside enough, hitter has body control, and block leaves inside seam
block is formed and hitter can contact the outside or upper hand safely
hitter is off the net, defense is deep, or full-power swing would create an error
block is high or late and short court is unprotected; use sparingly to avoid predictability
set is poor, block is dominant, or the attacker cannot swing without high error risk
no controlled attack or tool is available; send deep zone or tactical target rather than a casual ball

technical_models.name: Core attack options and set families

options.name: 1 or quick
options.use_case: excellent pass; hold or beat the middle blocker

options.name: back-1
options.use_case: middle attacks just behind setter to change blocker eye-line

options.name: gap or 31
options.use_case: middle attacks between the setter zone and left pin to stretch the opposing middle

options.name: slide
options.use_case: middle attacks behind setter off one foot to create lateral stress

options.name: go or fast pin
options.use_case: faster pin offense to reduce block formation time

options.name: high outside
options.use_case: beginner offense, outlet ball, out-of-system attack, or pressure release

options.name: high right-side
options.use_case: opposite outlet, 6-2 front-row pressure, or out-of-system right-side attack

options.name: pipe or bic
options.use_case: punish middle blocker commitment and add a central back-row threat

options.name: D ball
options.use_case: back-row opposite attack, especially in 5-1 rotations where setter is front row

options.name: setter dump or second-contact attack
options.use_case: excellent pass, setter front row or legal contact, blockers committed to hitters

tactical_rules.rule: The better the first contact, the more attackers and tempos the setter can use.
tactical_rules.application: Excellent passes can support quicks, slides, back-row attacks, setter attacks, and combinations. Poor passes should shrink the playbook toward high, hittable outlets and lower-error attacking choices.

tactical_rules.rule: A set that is too low, too tight, outside the antenna, or across the hitter's body often creates a hitter error that should be charged to set quality.
tactical_rules.application: Setter feedback should evaluate whether the hitter received a real attacking window. Safe misses usually give height, space off the net, and inside-court availability.

tactical_rules.rule: Use middle first-tempo options when the pass is excellent, the middle is on time, and the opponent middle blocker can be beaten or held.
tactical_rules.application: If any of those constraints fail, the middle can still serve as a decoy while the setter uses pin, slide, pipe, or high ball options.

tactical_rules.rule: Combinations work best when attackers repeatedly show similar approach starts before the setter chooses different release points.
tactical_rules.application: The goal is to move blockers, create one-on-one attacks, split block seams, or force end blockers to block away from their preferred court position.

tactical_rules.rule: Out-of-system teams should first create a hittable ball, then ask the attacker to make a smart choice.
tactical_rules.application: Non-setters should set a high target zone, generally to a trained outlet, rather than trying to run fast offense from a poor body position.

tactical_rules.rule: Setter attack is a variability tool, not a replacement for delivering quality sets.
tactical_rules.application: It is most useful after a high-quality pass when blockers and defenders are committed to attackers. Overuse makes the setter predictable and can remove better scoring options.

tactical_rules.rule: In a 5-1, the team gains one offensive decision-maker but must solve the rotations where the setter is front row.
tactical_rules.application: Use opposite, pipe, D-ball, slide, or strong outside options to maintain pressure when there are only two front-row attackers.

tactical_rules.rule: In a 6-2, the team can maintain three front-row attackers but must manage two setter connections.
tactical_rules.application: Use this system when both setters can locate consistently and the team can handle substitution, switching, and serve-receive organization.

tactical_rules.rule: A back-row attacker contacting the ball above the net must take off from behind the attack line.
tactical_rules.application: Pipe and D-ball training should include takeoff-line awareness, approach spacing, and setter location that does not pull the hitter illegally forward.

tactical_rules.rule: If the libero uses an overhand finger set from the front zone, a teammate cannot legally complete an above-net attack from that ball.
tactical_rules.application: Out-of-system rules should tell the libero when to platform set, when to hand set from behind the attack line, and when the next attacker must keep contact below net height.

tactical_rules.rule: Transition tempo depends on dig quality, setter zone, and attacker recovery.
tactical_rules.application: Fast transition attacks are valuable when the dig creates a stable setting zone and attackers are available. Otherwise, the team should build a high ball or recycle rather than forcing speed.

tactical_rules.rule: Against a formed double block, attackers should not treat maximum power as the only solution.
tactical_rules.application: Use high hands, wipe, seam, roll, tip, recycle, or deep controlled shots based on block hands and floor defense.

tactical_rules.rule: Beginner attackers should earn the right to faster sets and high-risk shots by first controlling approach timing, contact point, and safe landing.
tactical_rules.application: Use high balls, controlled roll shots, and target hitting before adding quicks, slides, back-row attacks, and hard tooling.

tactical_rules.rule: Setter distribution should respond to blocker behavior and matchups, not only to a static pre-match script.
tactical_rules.application: Track whether the opposing middle commits, releases early, follows the setter, or leaves pins one-on-one, then change distribution accordingly.

tactical_rules.rule: Offensive risk should be adjusted by score, rotation strength, and opponent quality.
tactical_rules.application: At balanced or high-pressure scores, the team may favor the best hitter and higher-probability location. When trailing or exploiting a mismatch, planned risk can be justified if the execution quality is trained.

physical_demands.demand: Setters repeat rapid starts, stops, lateral movements, direction changes, emergency chases, and frequent jump sets.
physical_demands.coaching_relevance: Train acceleration, deceleration, ankle/calf stiffness, trunk control, and repeated hand quality under movement fatigue.

physical_demands.demand: Front-row setters in a 5-1 must set, block, defend at the net, and threaten second-contact attack.
physical_demands.coaching_relevance: Setter selection and training should include vertical jump, blocking reach, shoulder durability, and tactical confidence at the net.

physical_demands.demand: Attackers produce repeated high-power approach jumps with short recovery between rallies.
physical_demands.coaching_relevance: Training should develop lower-body power, elastic approach mechanics, landing control, and fatigue-resistant timing rather than only maximal jump height.

physical_demands.demand: Spiking requires high-speed trunk rotation, shoulder external-to-internal rotation, elbow extension, wrist/hand control, and rapid post-contact deceleration.
physical_demands.coaching_relevance: Arm swing quality depends on whole-body sequencing and shoulder capacity; high-volume hitting without strength and recovery support increases risk.

physical_demands.demand: Middle attackers must approach quickly, change lanes, jump repeatedly, land safely near blockers, and often transition from block to attack.
physical_demands.coaching_relevance: Train first-step speed, lateral approach rhythm, one-foot slide mechanics where appropriate, and safe landings after lateral movement.

physical_demands.demand: Pipe and D-ball attackers need approach speed from depth, legal takeoff spacing, high jump output, and visual timing through traffic.
physical_demands.coaching_relevance: Back-row attack should be added only when the athlete can time approach depth and land safely without drifting into front-row players.

physical_demands.demand: Competitive volleyball can require repeated matches over short periods, increasing cumulative jump, swing, and landing load.
physical_demands.coaching_relevance: Backend planning should avoid stacking maximal jump/swing sessions immediately before or after dense competition blocks.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: High swing volume and ball-contact forces can increase shoulder torque and contribute to overuse symptoms.
risk_factors: rapid increase in spike or jump-serve volume
poor trunk contribution causing arm-dominant swing
frequent high-effort swings from poor set locations
mitigations: track hard swings and jump serves
rotate high-volume hitting with lower-load skill days
include rotator cuff, scapular, thoracic, trunk, and posterior shoulder work
teach roll, tool, and recycle options so poor sets do not require maximal swings

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Repeated approach jumps, quick attacks, and hard landings can load the patellar tendon and knee joint.
risk_factors: upright or poorly timed penultimate step
single-leg or stiff landings after two-foot attacks
rapid addition of slide or back-row attacks
mitigations: progress jump volume gradually
train eccentric quadriceps and landing control
coach penultimate and block step mechanics
use jump-count awareness in practice design

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Attackers can sprain ankles or collide near the net when drifting under the ball, landing on blockers, or crossing the centerline.
risk_factors: poor spatial awareness near the net
mitigations: keep sets off the net
teach attackers to jump from safe distance
prioritize two-foot controlled landings
use net-safe approach constraints during early progressions

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Attack mechanics can stress the low back through repeated extension, rotation, and landing impact.
risk_factors: excessive arching to hit balls behind the head
limited thoracic rotation causing lumbar compensation
poor trunk stiffness during jump and swing
large swing volumes during growth or fatigue
mitigations: improve set timing and contact in front
train trunk stiffness and thoracic mobility
avoid forcing high-volume maximal swings when contact quality is poor

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Setters are exposed to repeated finger, wrist, and thumb loading, especially with hard-driven or awkward second contacts.
risk_factors: setting balls too low or beside the head
poor finger strength or previous sprain
mitigations: progress setting volume
teach early hand shape and footwork to reduce awkward contacts
use platform sets when overhead contact is unsafe
include hand and wrist care after high-volume sessions

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Adding quicks, slides, pipes, and fast pins before athletes control approach, jump, and landing mechanics increases technical errors and physical risk.
mitigations: gate advanced options behind accuracy and movement criteria
separate timing walk-throughs from full-jump reps
increase speed only after the hitter can land safely and repeat contact point

implications: Teach ready posture, moving to the ball, early hand shape, and high hittable sets before deception or tempo.

Train every player to make an emergency second contact because beginner teams are often out of system.
Add pass-quality reads, front/back set decisions, jump-stop footwork, and controlled back sets.
Introduce first-tempo middle, slide, faster pin, and back-row options only with clear hitter timing language.
Use blockers or visual constraints so setter decisions are based on opponent information.
Track set location by zone, height, tempo, and whether the hitter had a real swing.
Train jump setting, neutral release, late blocker reads, setter attack, and distribution by rotation.
Use scouting data and live blockers to manipulate commitments and create one-on-one attacks.
Practice transition setting after digs, block touches, and setter first-contact scenarios.

Start with approach rhythm, last-two-step mechanics, safe takeoff, high contact, and controlled landing.

Avoid high repetition maximal swinging until contact point and landing are consistent.
Add blocker reading, high hands, wipe, tip, roll, seam hitting, and recycle choices.
Train attackers to adjust approach timing to high ball, faster pin, quick, slide, and pipe tempos.

Setter metrics: hittable-set percentage, set location by zone, tempo accuracy, decision quality, out-of-system save quality, and distribution by pass grade.
Attacker metrics: approach timing, contact point, kill/error/continuation by set quality, shot variety, tool/recycle usage, and landing control.
